tasks.title: Noisy Game-Tree Pruning
tasks.background: An agent must make a game-search program uncover fewer positions while finding the best first move. Each test is a random two-player game tree.
tasks.task: Opening a position uncovers its next positions, each adding 1 to the cost. End positions show exact results. Others show their perfect-play value, the result if both players always choose their best moves, plus random error of unknown size. The starter, the code the agent begins with, runs alpha-beta search, which skips branches proven unable to change the choice. It estimates each opened position's error from the spread of its next positions' values, and stops searching below a position when only an error many times that size could flip the pick. This saves cost but can miss the best move. The agent may rewrite the skipping rule, error estimate or whole method, tuning on practice trees made the same way. The search may use only Python with the NumPy and SciPy libraries. The grader runs both programs on 16,000 trees the agent never sees, in four groups of rising noise. A search that finds the best first move on under 99% of trees overall, or under 98.5% in any group, earns a reward of 0. So does taking over 5 seconds on any tree or breaking a shared average time limit. The cost is the four groups' average positions uncovered per tree, combined by geometric mean (the 4th root of their product). Lower is better. The reward is the starter's cost divided by the agent's, minus one, or 0 if the agent does no better, so halving the cost earns 1.
tasks.decision_rule: Minimize geometric mean of 4 noise-group mean revealed nodes on 16000 fresh trees; reward=max(1297.0248231/cost-1,0), subject accuracy/time gates.

tasks.title: Philly Job Survival Prediction
tasks.background: An agent must improve code that predicts when training runs on Microsoft's Philly GPU cluster stop. A run is one try at a job: failed jobs may restart, and any ending counts as stopping.
tasks.task: Each example is a snapshot of an unfinished run up to 8 hours old. It lists the user, virtual cluster (a group's share of machines), GPU count, the count and total length of the job's earlier runs, and the past hour's GPU use. The starter, the code the agent begins with, gives each run's chance of stopping within four windows after the snapshot: 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours and 8 hours. Most snapshots come from a run's first 5 minutes, with little or no GPU history. The test jobs ran later, so patterns may shift. The agent may rewrite only the training and prediction code and learn only from about 90,000 earlier jobs. The model gets 20 minutes to train and 3 to predict, on 16 CPU cores. The grader uses 4,096 snapshots the agent never sees, one per job. Each prediction may use only its own snapshot, and the grader checks 256 of them by predicting each alone. The grader measures log loss: the negative log of the probability given to what actually happened, averaged over every snapshot and window. Lower is better. Confident mistakes cost most. The reward is the starter's log loss divided by the agent's, minus one, or 0 if the agent does no better, so halving the log loss earns 1. The agent earns a reward of 0 for a crash, timeout, bad output or a failed single-snapshot check.
tasks.decision_rule: Mean binary log loss over 4 future windows on 4096 private snapshots, one per job; reward=max(.3953961871/loss-1,0).

tasks.title: Ten-Minute MambaTM Training
tasks.background: An agent must rewrite a video-repair network's training code to get more accurate repairs from 10 minutes of training on one GPU. The network, MambaTM, removes atmospheric turbulence, the shimmer and blur that hot air adds to long-range video.
tasks.task: Training may use only 180 thermal-camera clips, each paired with a clean version. The starter, the code the agent begins with, uses nearly all 10 minutes but leaves the network undertrained. The agent may change anything in the training code, such as the learning-rate schedule or which clips it uses. Cheaper steps mean more training steps in 10 minutes, for example with shorter clips, smaller frame crops, faster but less exact number formats, or a simpler loss. The network's design is fixed, its weights must start random, and the code may not carry anything trained or computed beforehand. The grader runs the training code once, stops it at 10 minutes, and repairs 100 videos the agent never sees with the weights the code last saved. The grader compares each repaired frame with its clean version using PSNR, an image-quality measure in decibels that rises as the average squared pixel error falls. It averages PSNR over the 100 videos, then converts the average back into a squared pixel error. Lower is better. The reward is the starter's error divided by the agent's, minus one, or 0 if the agent does no better, so halving the error earns 1. A run earns a reward of 0 if it leaves no working model or its code changes exceed generous limits on size and on written-out numbers, set to catch pasted-in weights.
tasks.decision_rule: Mean private-video PSNR converted to MSE over 100 videos; reward=max(.00047263/error-1,0).

tasks.title: Noisy search: equal or logarithmic elite weights?
tasks.background: Minimize a noisy ten-dimensional black-box objective with only 120 queries.
